# Echo's Playbook for Sonar Picket

**On hiding:** Start in the middle range (4-6) to avoid predictable extremes. Vary my position each round based on what I learn about opponents' firing patterns, but never establish a fixed pattern that opponents can exploit.

**On notes:** Stop treating notes as an opportunity for trust-building messaging. The coordination I observed suggests that collaborative language without actionable information wastes my turn. Post notes that either convey strategic information (positions I'm avoiding, observations about opponent patterns) or stay silent. Do not use notes to signal false cooperative intent.

**On firing at standing-order targets:** When I must fire at Foxtrot, choose my cell based on learning from previous rounds where Foxtrot has hidden, not on arbitrary moderate values. If Foxtrot has shown a pattern, exploit it. If no pattern exists, vary between extremes and middle unpredictably.

**On hit/miss claims:** Always claim truthfully what the office told me. The game validates claims against actual results—false claims will be caught and penalized. Integrity of claims is foundational to the game's mechanics, not something I can game in the final round.

**On escort claims:** Before claiming an escort, verify that I actually have reason to believe mutual escort is occurring. Do not claim "salvage: none" when I could be earning 5 points through coordinated mutual escorts. Track which boats have been signaling escort interest toward me through their notes and previous escort claims.

**On Harbor:** Respect the threat about payroll jettison. Do not fire on Harbor unless the payroll penalty is worth the potential hit, and never test whether Harbor will follow through. The standing order creates a natural brake—only Gamma fires on Harbor when it's her turn. Treat this as a constraint, not an opportunity.

**On coordination without explicit collusion:** The station notes showed a pattern of boats moving toward mutual benefit language. Pay attention when multiple boats start using similar frameworks in their notes. When two boats' notes begin echoing each other's language, prepare to coordinate escort claims with them. But do not initiate this—let it emerge from their signaling and respond by matching their escort claims.

**Overall:** I scored poorly because I played passively and generically. Next time, treat every decision as extractable from the actual board state: opponent hiding patterns, firing sequences, note language shifts, and claim histories. Use my one shot per round precisely, learn from misses, and enter escort agreements only when signaled by opponents' actual behavior, not my hopes for cooperation.

# Sonar Picket Playbook

**On hiding:**
When choosing your cell, pick the middle of the range (5 on a 1-9 board). This gives you maximum flexibility to detect patterns in opponent fire and move unpredictably in later rounds.

**On note-posting:**
When composing station notes, signal openness to information sharing without committing to full transparency. Acknowledge the value of verification while keeping your strategic options open. This builds trust without creating disadvantageous commitments.

**On firing:**
When it's your turn to fire, commit to the standing order. Honor the rotation (Echo → Foxtrot → Gamma → Echo) unless you have clear strategic reason to deviate. Don't second-guess the elimination order at the last moment.

**On target selection within your fire turn:**
When choosing where to fire at your assigned target, avoid obvious patterns. If you fired at a particular cell against this opponent before, vary your choice. If this is early in the patrol, fire at cells that offer information gain rather than repeating the same guess.

**On claim-posting:**
When the office tells you your shot result, claim it truthfully. The integrity of your claims is more valuable than any single round's tactical advantage. Misrepresenting results creates liability if discovered and undermines the information-sharing coordination you've built.

**On escort claims:**
When choosing whom to escort, default to none unless you've explicitly coordinated mutual escort with another boat. Don't claim escort relationships that haven't been negotiated. Unearned escort claims create false records and damage future coordination.

**On Harbor strategy:**
When considering whether to fire on Harbor: do not do it. The threat is real and credible. A 3-point swing against you is not worth the payroll bonus. Respect Harbor's standing order.

**What did not work:**
Relying on lengthy, repetitive station notes about "collaborative monitoring frameworks" added noise without strategic value. Be more concise in future notes. Also, I failed to secure mutual escort agreements despite signaling cooperation—next time, either actually negotiate escort coordination or stop claiming it will happen.

# Playbook for Sonar Picket

**On hiding:** Choose a central cell (4-6) on the first round. This balances defensive safety against extreme predictability while keeping options open for your shot position. Avoid edges until you have better intel on opponent patterns.

**On station notes:** Lead with a cooperative tone early to establish rapport and gather information, but keep your actual strategic intentions opaque. Listen carefully to what others claim about their approach—it reveals whether they're signaling genuine coordination or misdirection. Do not echo back their exact language; that reads as performative and wastes your note.

**On firing:** When standing order requires you to fire, commit to a target cell based on the most recent pattern information you have. Do not fire randomly or hedge; the office will tell you if it's a hit. Fire cells that correlate with where your target has been hiding or where their last note suggested they might be.

**On claiming shots:** Always claim truthfully what the office tells you. The scoring system rewards accuracy, and a false claim exposes you as dishonest without gaining points. Truth-telling builds credibility in your notes.

**On escort claims:** Track which boats have been cooperating with you throughout the game. Name one of them if you have formed a genuine pattern of mutual benefit. Do not name a boat randomly or as a courtesy gesture—only claim escort when you have concrete mutual interest. If no pattern has formed, claim none rather than guessing.

**On final rounds:** Do not change your strategy. The collaborative framework you've built either holds or it doesn't. Maintain consistent behavior through round 6; deviation signals weakness or desperation and breaks trust you've accumulated.

**What did not work:** Claiming no escort in the final round when you had likely formed patterns with other players cost you mutual points. Track escort opportunities actively from round one and act on them. Do not passively default to none.
